title: Orthostatic Assessment: Symptoms, Technique, and Fall Risk
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Orthostatic assessment is more than comparing blood-pressure numbers. The PN/LVN should connect position change with symptoms, pulse/BP response, hydration, medication exposure, fall risk, and the patient's ability to stand safely.
recognize: Lightheadedness, weakness, blurred vision, near-syncope or falls after standing can reflect orthostatic intolerance even when one reading is equivocal.
Diuretics, vasodilators, alpha blockers, dehydration, blood loss and autonomic dysfunction can contribute.
priorities: Use the facility's standardized measurement technique and guard the patient from falling during position changes.
Escalate syncope, chest pain, new neurologic findings, active bleeding, shock signs, or persistent symptomatic hypotension.
assessMonitor: Trend supine/seated/standing BP and pulse per protocol, symptoms, hydration, medications, gait and recent falls.
interventions: Assist with gradual position changes, reinforce hydration plan when appropriate, and implement individualized fall precautions.
medicationSafety: Do not independently stop antihypertensives or diuretics; report symptomatic trends for medication review.
teaching: Rise slowly, pause before walking, and report recurrent dizziness or fainting.
delegationScope: Vital-sign collection may be delegated when appropriate; interpreting symptomatic orthostasis and escalating instability remain licensed-nurse responsibilities.
examTrap: Recording an orthostatic drop while allowing a dizzy patient to walk unassisted back to bed.
oneLinePearl: Orthostatics are a fall-risk assessment with hemodynamics attached.
sourceBasis: AHRQ hospital fall-prevention resources and orthostatic vital-sign measurement tools

title: Pulse Oximetry: Trust the Patient More Than One Number
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
bottomLine: Pulse oximetry estimates oxygen saturation but can be inaccurate. Clinical deterioration, poor perfusion, motion, nail products, skin temperature, device quality and skin pigmentation can affect interpretation, so the patient's work of breathing and overall status must remain central.
recognize: A reassuring SpO2 does not exclude respiratory failure when the patient is tiring, confused, cyanotic or showing increased work of breathing.
FDA materials continue to warn that performance can vary across skin pigmentation and under low-perfusion or other adverse measurement conditions.
priorities: Verify sensor placement and signal quality, assess respiratory effort and perfusion, and compare the reading with the clinical picture.
Escalate unexplained discordance or deterioration rather than repeatedly adjusting the probe without clinical action.
assessMonitor: Trend SpO2, respiratory rate/effort, mental status, perfusion, oxygen device/settings and response to therapy.
interventions: Correct obvious measurement problems and obtain ordered confirmatory testing when the clinical picture and oximetry disagree.
medicationSafety: Sedatives and opioids can depress ventilation before dramatic desaturation is apparent, especially with supplemental oxygen.
teaching: Home pulse-ox readings should be interpreted with symptoms and clinician instructions, not used as the only safety check.
delegationScope: Measurement can often be delegated; interpretation of abnormal or discordant findings and escalation remain licensed-nurse responsibilities.
examTrap: Choosing the normal pulse-ox number over obvious respiratory deterioration.
oneLinePearl: A pulse oximeter measures light absorption—not the whole patient.
sourceBasis: FDA pulse-oximeter performance guidance and safety communications

title: Respiratory Deterioration: Rate, Effort, Voice, and Fatigue
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Respiratory rate and work of breathing often deteriorate before blood pressure or oxygen saturation collapses. Accessory-muscle use, inability to speak normally, altered mentation, weak respiratory effort, and exhaustion are escalation cues.
recognize: Tachypnea with retractions/accessory-muscle use suggests increased work; a suddenly slower, shallow pattern in an exhausted patient can be worse, not better.
New agitation or somnolence may signal hypoxemia, hypercapnia, medication effect or fatigue.
priorities: Assess airway, breathing pattern, oxygen delivery, mental status and ability to speak; position and apply ordered support while escalating deterioration.
Do not delay urgent help for a complete routine assessment.
assessMonitor: Trend respiratory rate/depth, effort, breath sounds, voice/speech, mental status, SpO2, oxygen requirement and response.
interventions: Position for ventilation, maintain ordered oxygen/device support, reduce exertion and activate escalation pathways when deterioration persists.
medicationSafety: Review opioids, sedatives and neuromuscular/respiratory depressants when rate or mental status changes.
teaching: Seek urgent help for severe breathlessness, blue/gray color, confusion or inability to speak normally.
delegationScope: Counting respirations may be delegated in stable patients; evaluating new respiratory distress and escalating it is a licensed-nurse responsibility.
examTrap: Interpreting a falling respiratory rate as improvement when the patient is becoming exhausted.
oneLinePearl: A tired chest can look quieter just before it fails.

title: Delirium Recognition: Acute Change Is a Medical Clue
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Psychosocial Integrity
bottomLine: Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance in attention and cognition. New confusion should trigger assessment for illness, hypoxia, infection, medications, pain, retention, constipation, dehydration and metabolic causes rather than being dismissed as dementia or aging.
recognize: Fluctuation, inattention, altered level of consciousness and abrupt change from baseline favor delirium over chronic dementia.
Hypoactive delirium can appear quiet or sleepy and is easy to miss.
priorities: Establish baseline from patient/family/chart, assess immediate physiologic threats, review medications and report the acute change.
Use orientation, sleep, mobility, sensory aids, hydration and pain control while the cause is evaluated.
assessMonitor: Trend attention, arousal, orientation, oxygenation, temperature, hydration, pain, elimination, glucose when indicated and medication exposure.
interventions: Provide calm orientation, glasses/hearing aids, day-night cues, mobility and safety supervision; treat reversible contributors through the care plan.
medicationSafety: Anticholinergics, sedatives, opioids and polypharmacy can precipitate or worsen delirium; avoid reflexive sedation without cause assessment.
teaching: Families should report sudden behavior or attention changes because they may be the first sign of illness.
delegationScope: Routine observation may be shared with assistive personnel; assessment and interpretation of acute cognitive change require licensed-nurse escalation.
examTrap: Calling new confusion 'baseline dementia' without confirming the patient's actual baseline.
oneLinePearl: Dementia is chronic; delirium is a change until proven otherwise.
sourceBasis: AHRQ patient-safety resources on delirium in hospitalized older adults

title: Peripheral Neurovascular Checks: Protect the Limb Before the Pulse Disappears
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
bottomLine: After fracture, cast, surgery, vascular injury or swelling, trend pain, sensation, movement, color, temperature, capillary refill and pulses. Severe escalating pain or neurologic change can indicate limb-threatening compromise before a pulse is lost.
recognize: Pain out of proportion, pain with passive stretch, paresthesia, increasing tenseness, weakness or pallor are concerning.
A palpable pulse does not rule out compartment syndrome.
priorities: Compare the affected limb with prior findings and the opposite side when appropriate.
Escalate rapidly worsening pain, sensory/motor loss, pallor/coolness or absent pulse immediately.
assessMonitor: Trend pain, sensation, movement, skin color/temperature, capillary refill, swelling and distal pulses per order/protocol.
interventions: Keep casts/dressings visible and protected, avoid constrictive positioning, and follow emergency escalation for suspected compartment or vascular compromise.
medicationSafety: Analgesia should not substitute for reassessment of worsening pain or neurovascular findings.
teaching: Report increasing pain, numbness, inability to move digits or color/temperature change immediately.
delegationScope: Routine observation can be shared, but interpretation of neurovascular change and escalation are licensed-nurse responsibilities.
examTrap: Waiting for pulselessness before treating severe pain and paresthesia as urgent.
oneLinePearl: A pulse can survive early compartment syndrome—pain and nerves may warn first.
sourceBasis: Contemporary U.S. orthopedic and nursing neurovascular-assessment principles

title: Pressure-Injury Risk: Inspect Skin, Then Change the Risk
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Pressure-injury prevention starts with systematic skin inspection plus risk-factor assessment. Immobility, moisture, friction/shear, poor nutrition/perfusion, devices and existing injury should drive an individualized prevention plan rather than a score alone.
recognize: Nonblanching erythema, persistent discoloration, warmth/coolness, bogginess, tenderness or device pressure can precede deeper injury.
Darker skin tones may show pressure injury through color change, temperature, texture or pain rather than obvious redness.
priorities: Inspect bony prominences and device contact areas, identify modifiable risk factors and implement the prescribed prevention bundle.
Escalate rapidly evolving discoloration, blistering, necrosis, severe pain or suspected deep tissue injury.
assessMonitor: Trend skin condition, mobility, moisture, nutrition, perfusion, device pressure and standardized risk assessment per facility policy.
interventions: Reposition/offload according to individualized plan, manage moisture, protect device sites, optimize nutrition/hydration orders and use support surfaces as prescribed.
medicationSafety: Sedatives, vasopressors and other drugs that reduce mobility or perfusion can increase skin risk and should inform prevention planning.
teaching: Patients and caregivers should report persistent skin color/temperature changes, pain or device pressure early.
delegationScope: Assistive personnel can report skin findings and perform assigned repositioning; licensed nurses remain responsible for assessment, interpretation and plan escalation.
examTrap: Treating the Braden score as the intervention instead of addressing the patient's actual risks.
oneLinePearl: The score finds risk; the care plan changes risk.
sourceBasis: AHRQ Pressure Injury Prevention in Hospitals Training Program

title: Fluid-Status Assessment: Build the Pattern From Multiple Cues
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: No single cue proves dehydration or overload. Weight trend, intake/output, urine concentration/output, edema, lung findings, BP/orthostasis, mucous membranes, perfusion and labs must be interpreted together and in context.
recognize: Rapid weight change can reflect fluid shift more reliably than isolated edema or skin turgor.
Older adults may have less reliable skin-turgor findings, so multiple cues are essential.
priorities: Use consistent daily weights and accurate intake/output when ordered, then connect trends with symptoms and examination.
Escalate oliguria, worsening dyspnea, hypotension, acute confusion or rapid unexplained weight change.
assessMonitor: Trend weight, I/O, urine output, BP/orthostasis, edema, lung sounds, mucous membranes, perfusion and ordered sodium/renal labs.
interventions: Implement prescribed fluid/sodium plan, protect against falls in volume depletion and position/support breathing in overload.
medicationSafety: Diuretics, IV fluids, steroids and renally active drugs can alter volume status; reconcile therapy when trends change.
teaching: Follow the individualized daily-weight and fluid-reporting plan rather than self-adjusting diuretics or fluids.
delegationScope: Weights and I/O can be delegated with clear parameters; interpreting trends and changing the care plan are licensed responsibilities.
examTrap: Diagnosing dehydration from skin turgor alone in an older adult.
oneLinePearl: Fluid status is a pattern, not a single sign.

title: Pain Reassessment: Did the Intervention Actually Work?
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Pain treatment is incomplete until response and adverse effects are reassessed. Use an appropriate self-report or behavioral tool, compare function and physiology, and investigate new or disproportionate pain rather than simply repeating analgesia.
recognize: Persistent severe or escalating pain despite expected treatment can signal a new complication.
Sedation, respiratory depression, hypotension or confusion can be treatment toxicity even when pain improves.
priorities: Reassess pain and function within the timeframe appropriate to the intervention and route.
Escalate disproportionate pain, new neurologic/vascular findings or opioid toxicity.
assessMonitor: Trend pain score/behavior, location/quality, function, sedation, respirations, BP and treatment response.
interventions: Combine ordered pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic measures and document the effect, not just administration.
medicationSafety: Do not give repeated opioids solely because the numeric pain score remains high when sedation or respiratory depression is increasing.
redFlags: New severe pain out of proportion
teaching: Report pain that changes character, becomes suddenly severe or is accompanied by new weakness, breathlessness or faintness.
delegationScope: Observation and comfort measures may be delegated; evaluation of response and medication-toxicity decisions remain licensed-nurse responsibilities.
examTrap: Charting 'pain medication given' without evaluating effectiveness or toxicity.
oneLinePearl: Administration is an action; reassessment proves whether it was the right action.

title: Focused Abdominal Assessment: Recognize the Acute Abdomen
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
bottomLine: Focused abdominal assessment should identify deterioration: increasing distention, guarding/rigidity, persistent vomiting, GI bleeding, severe localized pain, absent passage of stool/flatus, fever, shock or sudden pain change require escalation rather than routine symptom treatment.
recognize: Pain with rigidity/guarding or hemodynamic instability is more concerning than isolated nausea or constipation.
Older adults and immunocompromised patients may have less dramatic tenderness despite serious disease.
priorities: Assess vital signs, pain pattern, distention, bowel function, vomiting/bleeding and hydration/perfusion.
Escalate peritoneal signs, shock, hematemesis/melena with instability, bilious vomiting in a child or suspected obstruction/perforation.
assessMonitor: Trend abdominal contour, tenderness, bowel function, emesis/stool characteristics, hydration, vitals and ordered labs.
interventions: Maintain prescribed NPO/IV/supportive plan and avoid unapproved oral intake or laxatives when obstruction/perforation is possible.
medicationSafety: Analgesics and antiemetics do not remove the need to reassess worsening abdominal pathology.
teaching: Seek urgent care for severe persistent abdominal pain with fainting, blood, repeated vomiting or a rigid/swollen abdomen.
delegationScope: Routine observations may be delegated; focused assessment of acute abdominal change and escalation are licensed-nurse responsibilities.
examTrap: Giving a laxative to a patient with distention, vomiting and no flatus before obstruction is evaluated.
oneLinePearl: When the abdomen becomes rigid, unstable or obstructed, stop treating symptoms and escalate the cause.
sourceBasis: Current U.S. acute-abdomen nursing assessment principles

title: After a Fall: Assess Injury Before Blaming the Fall Score
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: After an inpatient fall, first assess for injury and physiologic causes, then identify contributing factors and modify prevention. A fall-risk score does not replace post-fall neurologic, pain, mobility, medication and environmental assessment.
recognize: Head strike, anticoagulant use, new confusion, focal deficit, severe pain or inability to bear weight increases concern for serious injury.
Falls can result from orthostasis, infection, hypoglycemia, medications, urgency, delirium or environmental hazards.
priorities: Assess immediate ABCs/injury, neurologic status, pain and mobility before moving the patient unless immediate danger requires it.
Escalate suspected head, spine, hip or internal injury and follow post-fall monitoring protocol.
assessMonitor: Trend neurologic status, vitals, pain, mobility, anticoagulant/antiplatelet exposure and symptoms according to risk/protocol.
interventions: Implement injury precautions, notify appropriate clinicians, document objectively and participate in a post-fall huddle/root-cause review.
medicationSafety: Review sedatives, antihypertensives, hypoglycemics, diuretics and other fall-risk medications after the event.
teaching: Patients should call for help with mobility after a fall until the cause and safe plan are reassessed.
delegationScope: Assistive personnel can summon help and maintain safety; post-fall assessment and escalation require licensed-nurse involvement.
examTrap: Completing an incident report before assessing the patient for injury.
oneLinePearl: After a fall: patient first, paperwork later.
sourceBasis: AHRQ Fall TIPS and Preventing Falls in Hospitals resources
